<reason>Side B (CON) ran the stronger, more decision-shaping case. The marketing-arithmetic clash (a $50M original still carrying $40-60M wide-release marketing against a capped ceiling) was raised in the opening, pressed in rebuttals and pressure questions, and PRO never supplied a pricing of its claimed benefits—CON correctly and memorably tagged this as "benefits asserted, costs conceded, arithmetic declined." PRO's refusal to name a hit rate was epistemically honest but left its case without a quantified comparison, and CON exploited it directly. CON also flipped PRO's acquisition concession into a dilemma (either acquisitions satisfy the motion and the mid-budget production case evaporates, or the risk stays unpriced) and closed with the damaging "status quo dressed as reform" frame. PRO's best work—reframing the test as the marginal dollar, countering "brand by another name," and distinguishing selection from allocation in the closing—was competent but mostly defensive and never neutralized the burden-of-proof and pricing pressure. CON suffered two clipped turns, a modest execution cost, but the visible arguments still dominated the decisive clash.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 (B2.4–B2.5), which converted PRO's concession that acquisitions "can constitute spending more on originals" into a self-dissolving dilemma for the motion, then reinforced it in Rebuttal 2 and the Closing while pairing it with the unanswered hit-rate pricing demand.</best_rebuttal>
